clinicalPearls: Typically presents within the first weeks to months of life in a well-appearing, thriving infant with mucousy, blood-streaked stools and no systemic upset.
Most commonly triggered by cow's milk protein, with soy a frequent co-trigger; it occurs in both breastfed and formula-fed infants.
In breastfed infants the offending proteins reach the gut via the maternal diet, so maternal elimination of cow's milk (and sometimes soy) is first-line rather than stopping breastfeeding.
It is a non-IgE-mediated hypersensitivity, so skin-prick tests and specific IgE are usually negative and are not required for diagnosis.
The infant remains systemically well without prominent vomiting, dehydration or shock, which distinguishes it from food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome (FPIES).
Rectal bleeding usually settles within days to a couple of weeks after the trigger protein is removed, supporting the diagnosis.
Diagnosis is clinical; endoscopy with biopsy is reserved for atypical or refractory cases and shows eosinophilic mucosal infiltration and lymphonodular hyperplasia.
Formula-fed infants generally respond to an extensively hydrolysed formula, reserving amino-acid formula for those who fail hydrolysate.
reference.pathophysiology: The condition is a non-IgE-mediated, predominantly cell-mediated hypersensitivity to ingested food proteins, most often cow's milk protein and less commonly soy, egg or other proteins. Antigen exposure, either directly through formula or indirectly through maternal dietary protein secreted into breast milk, drives an eosinophil-predominant inflammatory infiltrate within the lamina propria of the distal colon and rectum. The resulting mucosal eosinophilia and lymphonodular hyperplasia render the mucosa friable, producing the characteristic low-grade bleeding and mucus. Inflammation remains localised to the gut without systemic features, and immunological tolerance to the offending protein typically develops during the first years of life.
additionalDifferentials: Swallowed maternal blood in the breastfed neonate (Apt-Downey test)
Infective colitis (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, shiga-toxin Escherichia coli)
Necrotising enterocolitis in the preterm or ill neonate
Vitamin K deficiency bleeding or coagulopathy
additionalInvestigations: Trial of dietary protein elimination (both diagnostic and therapeutic)
Stool microscopy and culture to exclude infective colitis
Full blood count with differential for peripheral eosinophilia and anaemia
Apt-Downey test to distinguish swallowed maternal blood in the neonate
Faecal calprotectin (raised but non-specific in early infancy)
Flexible sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy with mucosal biopsy in atypical or refractory disease
Coagulation studies if bleeding is unexpectedly brisk
redFlags: Faltering growth, poor weight gain or weight loss
Vomiting, lethargy, pallor, dehydration or shock suggesting FPIES or an alternative diagnosis
Brisk or large-volume rectal bleeding, or clinically significant anaemia
Abdominal distension, bilious vomiting or systemic toxicity suggesting surgical or obstructive pathology
Onset outside the typical infant age range or persistence despite thorough protein elimination
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and self-limiting, with most infants developing tolerance to the offending protein and successful dietary reintroduction between one and three years of age. Growth and long-term gut health are unaffected.
pitfalls: Attributing all infant rectal bleeding to allergy and missing an anal fissure or an infective or surgical cause.
Ordering IgE-based allergy tests, which are typically negative in this non-IgE-mediated condition and can mislead.
Stopping breastfeeding prematurely rather than trialling maternal dietary elimination.
Incomplete maternal elimination with hidden milk or soy, producing apparent treatment failure.
Failing to attempt planned reintroduction, leading to unnecessary prolonged dietary restriction.
references: ESPGHAN guidance on the diagnosis and management of cow's milk protein allergy
management: Eliminate cow's milk protein by maternal dietary exclusion of cow's milk, and often soy, while continuing breastfeeding
Extensively hydrolysed or amino-acid formula for formula-fed infants
Reassure parents given the benign, self-limiting course in a well, thriving infant
Confirm the diagnosis clinically as rectal bleeding settles within days to a couple of weeks after the trigger protein is removed
Monitor growth and resolution of bleeding, and correct any iron-deficiency anaemia
Planned, supervised reintroduction of the offending protein after a period to confirm acquired tolerance
Paediatric and dietitian input to support maternal nutrition on the elimination diet, escalating if systemic upset suggests food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome or another diagnosis
